prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean case of a physical idea (magic-wavelength trapping, so that the light shift cancels while many atoms are interrogated at once) that was demonstrated by Katori and then pushed by Ye's group to systematic uncertainty and stability near 10^-18, with many-body clock physics and cavity and comb technology doing real work. It has been reproduced in many independent laboratories and compared across sites, it has already enabled millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements and bounds on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and it is the technical basis of the pending redefinition of the second. Four colleagues placed it first and two placed it second, which tells me the breadth of support is genuine and not an accident of ranking rules. It is a measurement result that nature can check, in the sense I value: a theorist embedded in experimental teams recognises the care about every physical detail that this work required. I ranked circuit QED first in my opening ballot, but that is the field I know best and where my judgment is most entangled with my community, so I give weight to the fact that colleagues with no stake in it converge on B001.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision timekeeping has been honoured twice recently (Hall and Hansch in 2005 for the comb, Wineland and Haroche in 2012 for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks), so a lattice-clock prize can be read as a refinement of an already recognised line rather than a new regime of physics. The pair is also a defensible but not unique attribution: the Paris, NIST, PTB and other groups built decisive pieces, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest application is still ahead. I am outside my own expertise on metrology priorities and I have not verified the exact order of the magic-wavelength proposal and the early strontium experiments.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B001 first because measurement precision limits what we can learn, and he notes that Hall and Hansch were honoured for the comb, so the lattice clock itself is not covered by an earlier prize. He also ranks circuit QED fourth and worries about overlap with the 2025 prize and with Devoret's role.
responses.response: I agree on both. The comb prize recognised the frequency ruler, whereas the lattice clock is a different idea about trapping and many-atom interrogation, so the overlap is smaller than it looks. On circuit QED I accept your Devoret point: the 2025 prize covered macroscopic quantum tunnelling and the energy quantisation that underlie the transmon, and a quick second circuit prize would look repetitive even though cQED is scientifically distinct. That is a reason for me to move B003 from first place to an alternative, where it would be better placed after a few years.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B001 first as a concrete instrument result that nature can check, but asks whether the committee will see it as a technological refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes and notes that other clock groups could be argued as decisive.
responses.response: I share your concern about refinement and think the citation should be written to avoid it: the discovery is the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and what it showed (uncertainty at 10^-18, gravitational redshift across a millimetre, many-body effects in the clock), not simply a better clock. I disagree somewhat that other groups create a serious attribution problem. The Paris, NIST and PTB teams made important contributions, but Katori's scheme and Ye's performance are the two steps that are hardest to substitute. If the committee wants to weigh them, the right place to test it is the priority record, which none of us has checked.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the two-dimensional melting theory (B006) first for its generality and simplicity, and he ranks magic-angle graphene (B017) last on his list as probably premature because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with you on B017: the discovery is solid and widely reproduced, but the pairing mechanism is open and the field is under ten years old, so I would not put it in the preferred configuration. On B006 I defer on the physics, but I would ask for the strongest evidence of robustness: you yourself note that experiments differ and some melting transitions are first order. A prize for a general mechanism should show that the hexatic scenario holds up as a physical result in several systems, and it is a candidate only supported by one member so far, so I would like to hear from you why the experimental record is strong enough.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as precision atomic physics she trusts, and she ranks optical-lattice quantum simulation (B042) second, though she notes that picking three of five names is difficult and may omit essential contributors.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking of B001 and with your reading of B042 as the strongest second candidate. I think the five-name problem is real: Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger carry the experiments I proposed, Zoller and Cirac carry the theory, and any three cuts a founder. That is why I keep B042 as an alternative and not in my preferred configuration. I do not think the attribution issue is bigger for B001, which has a clean two-name credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the redefinition of the second should be well advanced before the prize is awarded, which is a timing judgment and not a scientific one.
Relative priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, the early strontium experiments and the contributions of other clock groups, which I have not independently verified.
How soon after the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize circuit QED could be recognised, and whether Girvin or Blais should be the fourth name if it were.
statement.conflict_note: I have a specific connection to B003 (circuit QED) and its credited names: I work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, and have Chalmers colleagues and WACQT guest researchers in the field, so I should recuse myself from deliberating on B003 and would not rely on my own opening first place for it. No specific connection to the credited names of B001, B042 or the other shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile.
